title: 'Time to abolish the Indian Act,' Manitoba premier tells PM in historic meeting with chiefs
summary: Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew is calling on the federal government to abolish the Indian Act, in a move that saw a warm reception from some but drew criticism elsewhere.

image.caption: Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew speaks with journalists during the meeting in Ottawa on Monday. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Manitoba
Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew is calling on the federal government to abolish the Indian Act, in a move that saw a warm reception from some but drew criticism elsewhere.
Carney says he shares Kinew's view, is 'committed' to moving Canada past Indian Act
Kinew shared that request publicly during a scrum in Ottawa on Monday, as First Nations leaders and Canada's first ministers met to discuss Indigenous rights for the first time in two decades.

"I don't know how many folks in Canada have seen one of these before, but this is a status card, and it says your friend Wab Kinew is an Indian, within the meaning of the Indian Act," he said, holding up his own card in front of reporters during a midday break in the historic meeting.
"I'm not sure if that lines up with your vision of Canada, that we still have a race-based form of identification in this country. But this is a reality."

Kinew, who is Anishinaabe from Onigaming First Nation in Ontario, said he raised the issue with Prime Minister Mark Carney earlier Monday, calling it "long overdue that we have a relationship with Indigenous Peoples in Canada that reflects who we are as Canadians today.
"I think it's time to abolish the Indian Act," Kinew said. "And it needs to be done with First Nations people and First Nations governments."
Later Monday, Carney said he shared Kinew's view and is "committed to a process that moves Canada beyond the Indian Act."
Manitoba premier calls for Indian Act to be scrapped
He said he's asked his ministers to work in partnership with First Nations to "chart that path together."
Speaking alongside Carney, Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak talked about the diversity of First Nations in provinces and territories across Canada.
Carney 'very open' to abolishing Indian Act

"And that question is going to be up to them to decide," she said. "I look forward to hearing from First Nations in assembly this December, right here in Ottawa," when the AFN hosts its special chiefs assembly in the capital.
Jerry Daniels, grand chief of the Southern Chiefs' Organization in Manitoba, said the sentiment Kinew shared has been heard for decades from First Nations leaders.

Jerry Daniels, grand chief of the Southern Chiefs' Organization in Manitoba, says it was 'refreshing' to hear a premier call for abolishing the Indian Act. (David Lipnowski/Southern Chiefs' Organization)
"I think the refreshing part of what we're hearing today is that we're now hearing it from a premier," he said in an interview.

But Sheila North, chief of Bunibonibee Cree Nation in Manitoba, said the consensus among chiefs she spoke to Monday was that it was "inappropriate" for Kinew to call to abolish the Indian Act. She said he represents a province that has been part of the "broken promises and unfinished business" First Nations have dealt with historically.
North, a former journalist with CBC News, said she wants to see changes to the Natural Resources Transfer Agreements, for example, which gave Prairie provinces control over natural resources.

"If you really are committed to changing the lives of our nations, let us have our own jurisdictions in our communities, and have our own, you know, rights upheld and our treaties respected when it comes to planning of our resources," she told CBC's Up to Speed host Faith Fundal.

Sheila North is chief of Bunibonibee Cree Nation in Manitoba. She says the consensus among chiefs she spoke to Monday was that Kinew's statements were 'inappropriate' because Manitoba has been part of the 'broken promises' First Nations have dealt with historically. (Trevor Brine/CBC)
The controversial Indian Act legislation has governed the lives of First Nations people for the last 150 years.
Coming into effect in 1876, the act controlled almost every aspect of First Nations people's lives, dictating things like how communities were governed and who could be considered an "Indian."
While the act has had many amendments, it remains the overarching legal document for First Nations in Canada.
'Nothing to lose but your chains'

Monday's closed-door meeting, which saw Carney and most of Canada's premiers sit down with chiefs from the Assembly of First Nations in Ottawa for a discussion, was the first such gathering since the Kelowna Accord talks of 2005.
That meeting brought premiers and then prime minister Paul Martin together with Indigenous leaders to discuss ways to close the socioeconomic gaps in Indigenous communities.

blocks.text: The Kelowna agreement was not implemented after the Conservative government under former prime minister Stephen Harper took office only a few months later.
Woodhouse Nepinak said Monday's meeting was intended to help build prosperity for coming generations.
It comes as Carney's government works to speed up major project approvals and development — efforts some First Nations chiefs have said threaten their rights.

Tensions between Ottawa and First Nations spiked soon after Carney was elected in 2025, when his government passed legislation to create a new office tasked with streamlining major project developments and approving projects within one year.
Kinew said Monday he supports Carney's work at the international level, "saying that we are going to be a leader when it comes to human rights and democracy, and a leader among middle powers."
But he called the Indian Act's continued existence inconsistent with that message.

blocks.text: The premier said though doing away with the Indian Act would bring changes, things like treaties and constitutional rights would still be able to exist for First Nations people.
"You can have self-determination, and you can have strong Indigenous nationhood, while at the same time not having the paternalism and the barriers that come with the Indian Act," Kinew said.
"You have nothing to lose but your chains."
